question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2022, developmental psychologist Ingrith Valbourne claimed that children aged 8 to 10 who speak two languages at home finish a card-sorting game that requires switching between sorting by color and sorting by shape faster than children who speak one language, because bilingual children are better at ignoring information that is irrelevant to the task at hand.
• A team led by Osric Tamlen at the Ashgrove Child Study Centre tested 36 children aged 8 to 10 who speak two languages at home and 36 children aged 8 to 10 who speak one language.
• The bilingual children finished the card-sorting game in an average of 142 seconds; the one-language children finished it in an average of 171 seconds.
• Each child also completed an arrow task in which a row of five arrows appeared on a screen and the child pressed the left or right key to match the direction of the middle arrow only.
• On some trials the four outer arrows pointed the same way as the middle arrow; on other trials they pointed the opposite way. The direction of the outer arrows never affected which key was correct.
• For each child, the team recorded how much slower the response was on opposite-direction trials than on same-direction trials. The average difference was 64 milliseconds for the bilingual children and 64 milliseconds for the one-language children.
• Both tasks were completed in a single session on a tablet computer.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Valbourne's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings bear out Valbourne's observation but not their explanation: the bilingual children finished the card-sorting game in an average of 142 seconds to the one-language children's 171 seconds, yet both groups responded an average of 64 milliseconds more slowly on opposite-direction arrow trials than on same-direction trials.
answer_b: The team's findings undermine Valbourne's claim: the bilingual children and the one-language children each responded an average of 64 milliseconds more slowly on opposite-direction arrow trials than on same-direction trials.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Valbourne's claim: the bilingual children finished the card-sorting game in an average of 142 seconds, compared with an average of 171 seconds for the one-language children.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Valbourne's claim and show the two groups were otherwise comparable: the bilingual children finished the card-sorting game in an average of 142 seconds to the one-language children's 171 seconds, and both groups responded an average of 64 milliseconds more slowly on opposite-direction arrow trials than on same-direction trials.
explanation: Choice A is the best answer because it matches each part of Valbourne's claim to the data that bears on it. Valbourne's sentence says two things: that bilingual children aged 8 to 10 finish the color-and-shape switching game faster than one-language children, and that this happens because bilingual children are better at ignoring information that is irrelevant to the task at hand. The card-sorting times bear on the first part. The bilingual children averaged 142 seconds and the one-language children averaged 171 seconds, so the faster finish Valbourne described did appear. The arrow task bears on the second part. In that task, the notes state that the direction of the outer arrows never affected which key was correct, so the outer arrows carry information that has no bearing on the right answer, and any slowdown when they point the opposite way shows that a child did not fully set them aside. A child who is better at setting such information aside would be slowed less when the outer arrows point the opposite way. The two groups were slowed by the same amount, an average of 64 milliseconds each, so there was no sign that the bilingual children were better at this. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the single session and the tablet computer describe the method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical 64-millisecond slowdowns do count against Valbourne's explanation, but the claim also says that bilingual children finish the card-sorting game faster, and the sorting times (142 seconds versus 171 seconds) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 142 versus 171 seconds do fit the first part of Valbourne's claim, that bilingual children finish the game faster, but the claim also says this happens because bilingual children are better at ignoring information that is irrelevant to the task, and the arrow-task results (a 64-millisecond slowdown in both groups) show no such advantage. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because it misreads the arrow-task result as a control rather than as a test of the explanation. In the arrow task only the middle arrow matters, and the notes state that the outer arrows never affected which key was correct, so the slowdown on opposite-direction trials shows how much information with no bearing on the task held a child back, which is what Valbourne's 'because' clause is about. The identical slowdowns (64 milliseconds in both groups) therefore show that the bilingual children did not handle the conflicting outer arrows any better, which fails to support the explanation instead of confirming it. Nothing in the notes presents the arrow task as a check that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the claim.

question_text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In 2022, avian ecologist Lucan Thorncombe claimed that tarnwing chickadees from harsh high-elevation forests recover more of the seeds they cache in autumn than tarnwing chickadees from mild lowland forests do, because the high-elevation birds keep better track of where things are.
• A team led by Bastien Aldreth at the Hartsgill Field Station housed 24 tarnwing chickadees from high-elevation forests and 24 tarnwing chickadees from lowland forests in separate aviaries and gave each bird 40 seeds to cache in October.
• Two weeks later, the team counted the cached seeds each bird retrieved: the high-elevation birds recovered an average of 62% of their cached seeds, and the lowland birds recovered an average of 38%.
• The team also tested the same 48 birds on an array of 8 feeders arranged in a circle, each holding one seed. Once a bird took a seed from a feeder, that feeder stayed empty for the rest of the trial.
• For each trial, the team recorded how many times the bird returned to a feeder it had already emptied before it had emptied all 8.
• The high-elevation birds averaged 2.4 such returns per trial, and the lowland birds averaged 2.4 such returns per trial.
• Each bird completed 5 trials of the feeder test, and all trials were run between 9 a.m. and noon.

The student wants to accurately characterize what the team's findings indicate about Thorncombe's claim. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
answer_a: The team's findings bear out Thorncombe's claim and show the two groups were otherwise comparable: the high-elevation chickadees recovered an average of 62% of their cached seeds to the lowland chickadees' 38%, and both groups averaged 2.4 returns to already-emptied feeders per trial.
answer_b: The team's findings undermine Thorncombe's claim: the high-elevation chickadees and the lowland chickadees averaged the same number of returns to already-emptied feeders per trial in the feeder test, 2.4.
answer_c: The team's findings bear out Thorncombe's claim: the high-elevation chickadees recovered an average of 62% of their cached seeds, compared with an average of 38% for the lowland chickadees.
answer_d: The team's findings bear out Thorncombe's observation but not their explanation: the high-elevation chickadees recovered an average of 62% of their cached seeds to the lowland chickadees' 38%, yet the two groups averaged the same number of returns to already-emptied feeders per trial, 2.4.
explanation: Choice D is the best answer because it matches each part of Thorncombe's claim to the data that bears on it. Thorncombe's sentence says two things: that high-elevation tarnwing chickadees recover more of the seeds they cache than lowland tarnwing chickadees do, and that this happens because the high-elevation birds keep better track of where things are. The caching results bear on the first part. The high-elevation birds recovered an average of 62% of their cached seeds, compared with 38% for the lowland birds, so the difference Thorncombe described did appear. The feeder test bears on the second part. Each feeder held one seed and stayed empty once a bird had taken it, so going back to an emptied feeder before all 8 were emptied is a wasted trip to a place the bird has already dealt with. A bird that keeps better track of where things are should make fewer of these returns. The high-elevation birds and the lowland birds both averaged 2.4 such returns per trial, so there was no sign that the high-elevation birds were better at this. The findings therefore bear out the observation but not the explanation. The notes about the number of trials per bird and the time of day the trials were run describe the method and do not bear on either part.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it misreads the feeder test as a check on the groups rather than as a test of the explanation. The notes describe the feeder test as a count of returns to feeders a bird had already emptied, which is the kind of behavior Thorncombe's 'because' clause is about. The identical averages (2.4 for both groups) therefore show no difference in how well the groups keep track of where things are, which fails to support the explanation instead of confirming it. Nothing in the notes presents the feeder test as a check that the groups were otherwise comparable. This is the pattern of reading a null result on the mechanism as added support for the claim.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as undermined on the strength of only one data note. The identical feeder-test averages (2.4 returns per trial for both groups) do count against Thorncombe's explanation, but the claim also says that high-elevation chickadees recover more of their cached seeds, and the caching results (62% versus 38%) are consistent with that part. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fails one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it treats the whole claim as borne out on the strength of only one data note. The 62% versus 38% recovery figures do fit the first part of Thorncombe's claim, that high-elevation chickadees recover more of their cached seeds, but the claim also says this happens because those birds keep better track of where things are, and the feeder test (2.4 returns to emptied feeders per trial for both groups) shows no such advantage. This is the pattern of citing accurate data that fits one part and generalizing it to the entire claim.
